UCUUUCUGCACCUUGUCGCTT-3’),
For the preparation of conditioned media, The cell lines of human umbilical vein

For Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays44, primary MSCs were cultured in
10 cm dishes until reaching 90% confluency. The cells were cross-linked by incubating in
1% formaldehyde at room temperature for 10 minutes, followed by the addition of 125
mM glycine and incubation for 2 minutes at 4°C to quench the reaction. Cells were
resuspended in 1 mL of Farnham lysis buffer (5 mM PIPES pH 8.0, 85 mM KCl, 0.5% NP-
40, 1 mM DTT, and Protease inhibitor cocktail (#P8340, Sigma]) for 10 minutes to isolate
nuclear material. Crude nuclear pellets were re-suspended with lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-
HCl pH 7.9, 1% SDS, 10 mM EDTA, 1mM DTT, and Protease inhibitor cocktail). Lysates
were sonicated into 150–300 bp fragments using the setting of 6 cycles of 30s on/60s off
with a Bioruptor (Diagenode) at maximum power. Lysates were centrifuged at 13,000 x g
for 10 min at 4°C to remove cell debris, then the supernatant were collected and diluted
1:10 with dilution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.9, 0.5% Triton X-100, 2 mM EDTA, 150
mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, and Protease inhibitor cocktail). Chromatin was pre-cleared by
adding 20 μL per mL Protein G Sepharose™ 4 Fast Flow (#17-0618-01, GE Healthcare
Bio-sciences) for 1h at 4°C and then incubated with anti-p65 antibody overnight (#8242,
Cell Signaling technology) at 4°C. Following overnight incubation, 80 μL washed Pierce
protein G beads were added and incubated for 2h at RT. Beads were captured by
centrifugation and then washed with low salt wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.9, 2 mM
EDTA, 125 mM NaCl, 0.05% SDS, 1% Triton X-100, and Protease inhibitor cocktail),
high salt wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.9, 2mM EDTA, 500 mM NaCl, 0.05% SDS,
1% Triton X-100, and Protease inhibitor cocktail), LiCl wash buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.9,
1 mM EDTA, 250 mM LiCl, 1% NP-40, 1% sodium deoxycholate, and Protease inhibitor
cocktail), and 1x Tris-EDTA (TE). Chromatin was eluted by elution buffer (100 mM sodium
bicarbonate, 1% SDS) for 15 min at RT. Crosslinks were reversed through addition of 5
M NaCl and incubation at 65°C overnight. RNA and protein were removed by incubation
with RNase (#11119915001, Roche) and proteinase K (#EO0491, ThermoFisher
Scientific). DNA was purified through Phenol:Chloroform:IsoAmyl (25:24:1) extraction and
Isopropanol precipitation. Purified DNA was resuspended in 20 μL ddH2O and subjected
to qPCR (ChIP-qPCR). The amount of each DNA sequence in ChIP samples was
calculated relative to input using the ΔCt method. The sequences of primers for ChIP-
qPCR are B.S._1 (Forward 5’-GGCTTGGAGCTCTCATTATCT-3’ and Reverse 5’-
GACTAGTAAGAGCATCATGCAC-3’), B.S._2 (Forward 5’-
TTCAACCTAGAGTCAGGCTG-3’ and Reverse 5’-TGCCTGCAACTTTATCGC-3’),
B.S._3 (Forward 5’-GCCTCACCTGATATTTTATGTGG-3’ and Reverse 5’-
AAAGCTGAAAATGGGGCTC-3’).

Bulk RNA sequencing and analysis
Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (#15596018CN, Thermo Fisher) from
indicated cells isolated from the femoral arteries using FACS, and was eluted in 10 µL of
sterile water. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed by Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China).
Briefly, SMARTer Ultra RNA Kit (#634936, Takara) was used to synthesize cDNA.
After library amplification, cDNA was tagmented and bar coded using TruePrep DNA
Library Prep Kit V2 (#TD503-02, Vazyme). The quantity and quality of final libraries were
evaluated using the Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer and Agilent 2100 bioanalyzer. Then cDNA
libraries were pooled and sequenced on the Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform using a 150
bp paired-end modality. The sequencing process utilized the Sequencing by Synthesis
(SBS) method, employing four fluorescently labeled dNTPs, DNA polymerase, and
sequencing primers.
The process of raw data was performed on Galaxy platform (https://usegalaxy.org/).
Quality Control was performed with FastQC (Version 0.12.1). After trimming low quality
sequences using Cutadapt (Version 4.9), RNA STAR (Version 2.7.11a) was used to map
reads to the mouse reference genome (GRCm38/mm10). Gene expression quantification
was performed using featureCounts (Version 2.0.3) against mouse Gencode version 20
annotations. Differential expression analysis was conducted with the DESeq2 package
(version 1.42.0) in R, and p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method
to manage the false discovery rate, ensuring statistically rigorous detection of differentially
expressed genes. The differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified between different
groups were analyzed for pathway enrichment. Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia
of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses, and Gene Set
Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) were performed using the ClusterProfiler package (version
4.10.1) in R. All bulk RNA-seq data have been deposited to GEO (GSE281009).

Single-cell RNA sequencing and analyses
For single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), arterial cell isolation from murine femoral
arteries at 2 days (D2) and 7 days (D7) post-surgery or Sham operations was performed
as described above. The resuspended cells were stained with 10 μg/mL DAPI (#BL105A,
Biosharp, 1:1000), filtered through a 40-μm cell strainer, and subjected to fluorescence-
activated cell sorting (FACS) using a Cytek Aurora CS to isolate singlets. For each
experimental condition, alive cells from 6 mice of the FAI or Sham group were pooled to
create one sample per group. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was conducted
by Berry Genomics (Beijing, China) using the Chromium Single Cell 3’ Reagent Kits v3
(10X Genomics) in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, cells with a
viability of over 85% were washed with 0.04% BSA in DPBS and resuspended to a
concentration of 700–1200 cells/μL. The cells were then encapsulated in droplets, each
containing a uniquely barcoded bead, enabling the reverse transcription of mRNA into
cDNA. The cDNA libraries were subsequently amplified and sequenced on the Illumina
NovaSeq platform. Raw sequencing data were processed using Illumina’s bcl2fastq
converter to generate FASTQ files for further analysis. All scRNA-seq data have been
deposited to GEO (GSE281008).
For scRNA-seq data analysis and visualization, the sequencing data were processed
into gene expression matrix with the CellRanger (version 7.2.0, 10X Genomics).
Downstream analysis of the data was performed with the R package Seurat (Version 5.0.1)
65. Genes expressed in fewer than three cells were removed. Cells with >300 expressed
genes, <6,000 expressed genes, mitochondrial gene content <10%, and unique
molecular identifier (UMI) counts <40,000 were retained for further analysis, yielding to
27,515 cells. Samples of the Sham, FAI_D2, and FAI_D7 conditions were integrated using
R package harmony (Version 1.2.0) 66. Gene expression counts were normalized using
Log-normalization with a scale factor of 10,000, and the top 2,000 genes were selected
for individual sample through the variance stabilizing transformation method. Principal
components analysis (PCA) was performed and unsupervised clustering was visualized
in Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plots with a resolution of 0.1,
based on the top ten principal components. Cell clusters were then annotated based on
the well-established markers. Differentially expressed genes among the identified cell
clusters were determined by FindMarkers function from the Seurat package. For pseudo-
temporal single-cell trajectory analysis, Monocle (Version 2.30.1) and Monocle3 (Version
1.3.7) was utilized to investigate developmental trajectories. CellChat (Version 2.1.2) 67
was used to identify cell-cell communications, and cell differentiation states were
predicted by CytoTRACE package (Version 0.3.3) 68. For cell-cell communication analysis,
the numbers, strengths, and probabilities of cell-cell interactions across cell types were
quantitatively computed using CellChat (Version 2.1.2) based on the curated ligand-
receptor interaction database (CellChatDB). The information on the analysis results was
provided in the Supplementary Data 4 and 5. Lipid metabolism signature score was
computed using the function of AddModuleScore. The gene sets used for the pathway
enrichment analyses in this study were listed in the Supplementary Data 6 and 7. A QC
summary of the single-cell RNA sequencing was provided in Supplementary table 4.

Human study
This study enrolled patients who underwent one-year angiographic follow-up after
second-generation DES implantation at the Department of Cardiology, Affiliated
Hangzhou First People’s Hospital of Westlake University between July and October 2025.
The cohort consisted of 25 patients with in-stent restenosis (ISR), define as ≥50%
diameter stenosis in the stented segment or its immediate 5 mm margins, and 25 control
patients without ISR. Patients with hepatic, renal disease, malignancy, acute inflammation,
or age<18 or >80 years were excluded. All samples were obtained from patients after
receipt of written informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The
study protocol was approved by the ethics committee of Affiliated Hangzhou First People’s
Hospital of Westlake University (approval ID-2025ZN282-1). The basic demographic
information of all participants enrolled in this study is presented in Supplementary Table
3. Plasma IL-33 and OPN protein levels were determined by a commercially available
human IL33 ELISA Kit (#EK133, Multi sciences) and human OPN ELISA Kit (#EK1135,
Multi Sciences) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was carried out as indicated in the figure legends. All data are
presented as the mean ± s.e.m. unless otherwise indicated in the figure legends. Data
variance was examined by F test or Bartlett’s test. The data meet the assumptions of the
indicated statistical analysis. All tests were performed as two sided. A p value less than
0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using
Microsoft Excel or GraphPad Prism 8.0 (GraphPad Software). All statistical information,
including p values, samples sizes and repetitions, are provided in Supplementary Data 3.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, the authors report on the role of fibroblast-macrophage interaction following femoral artery endovascular injury in mice. The authors identify a pathway involving IL33-ST2-OPN in the regulation of macrophage activity that promotes neointimal hyperplasia after injury. This study is data intensive and experiments were generally well performed and well described. However, the scRNAseq data are superficially analyzed/described, additional data are needed to verify that perturbations have intended effects, gating strategies for flow cytometry need to be reported and quantification strategies justified, some data are overinterpreted and data presentation could be improved.
Major comments
1. In the Introduction, authors claim that factors regulating macrophage phenotype switching remain unclear. However, numerous studies implicate many potential candidates including cytokines, signaling pathways, growth factors. Please acknowledge this previous work and summarize current understanding.
2. Several datasets, including published scRNAseq data, were used in this study. It is difficult to follow which dataset was used for analysis in several figures. Please clarify the source of data used to generate each graph in each Figure.
3. Flow cytometry data and presentation should be improved. First, enzymatic tissue digestion causes significant cell death. Therefore, live/dead cell staining should be used in all flow analysis to allow gating out of dead cells from analysis. In addition, complete gating strategies for all flow cytometry analyses should be provided either in main or supplementary Figures. When presenting flow data as cell numbers, authors chose to normalize to per cm artery. Please justify this choice, as the obvious change in artery thickness could be expected to influence cell numbers. When presenting flow data as percentages, please clarify the denominator cell population in the calculation (e.g. total cells or immediate parent cell gate). Finally, please clarify which flow cytometry antibodies were used to identify immune cell populations in Figure 1 and how these correspond to the populations identified in the scRNAseq data.
4. scRNAseq analysis is overall superficial and/or incomplete. For data in Figure 1 and Extended Figure 1, please provide a more complete list of marker genes that differentiate both major cell clusters and immune cell subclusters for all datasets analyzed. Along these lines, please discuss how CD72 and CD63 were chosen as markers to discriminate macrophage clusters; these markers do not appear to be differentially expressed to a substantial level in the single cell data.
For all pathway analyses, please provide complete gene list as supportive data for each pathway identified.
For pseudotime analysis, cluster 1 macrophages are distributed across all pseudotime branches. Please discuss the potential significance of the presence of this apparently pro-inflammatory population over all pseudotime states. Since cluster 2 macrophages tend to have higher pseudotimes, one could infer that there may be a transition from cluster 1 to 2 macrophages. Please discuss. For Monocle 3 analyses, please indicate which cluster was selected as starting cluster. In addition to the pseudotime analysis, scRNA velocity analysis would provide additional insight into potential cell state transitions.
For the CellChat analysis, only numbers of interactions between cell clusters is presented. The strength of these interactions should also be presented as is likely less prone to false positives. In general, this analysis should be discussed more fully. As is, it is not clear whether this analysis was used to guide downstream experiments and a full appreciation of potential signaling networks involved is missing. Along these lines, please provide rationale to support choosing IL33 as a primary target. A discussion of other possible candidates from the scRNAseq data is warranted
In Extended Figure 3C, Trem2 expression appears to be high in both cluster 1 and 2 macrophages, which is inconsistent with flow data. Please discuss this discrepancy
5. For cell tracking and perturbation experiments, additional data are needed to verify effects on target cells and their specificity. For experiments with CX3CR1-GFP mice and CX3CR1-DTR mice, specificity of targeting macrophages should be demonstrated. CX3CR1 is expressed on many cell types, including other immune cells and fibroblasts, which could confound interpretation of these experiments. In addition, for the Ki20227 CSF1R inhibitor experiments, please show impact on monocyte/macrophage accumulation via flow cytometry. For Pdgfrb-CreER-IL33 mice, please demonstrate specificity of knockout to fibroblasts and lack of leakiness of knockout phenotype. For LysM-IL1RL1 mice, please demonstrate specificity of knockout to macrophages; neutrophils also express ST2 and osteopontin.
6. For the lineage tracing experiment using GFP mice (Figure 2g),it appears that the gating of GFP+ cells in the right panel should be moved to the right to the point showing clear separation between GFP+ vs GFP- cells. Negative cell fluorescence levels can be shifted between control and treated groups due to differing effects of compensation (due to lack of one color in control). Therefore, it is possible that the actual GFP+ cell proportion was less than 80% and a significant part of cluster 2 macrophages could come from transition from resident or cluster 1 cells. Additionally, please provide evidence(markers) to identify GFP+ cells as cluster 2 macrophages.
7. For the co-culture experiments, authors should justify use of HUVEC instead of primary mouse endothelial cells, and PDGFRb+ cells isolated from inguinal adipose tissue instead of from vessels. Also, authors should identify source of VSMC.
8. A paragraph on the limitations of the study is missing. Please add.
Minor comments
9. In Extended Figure 1a, please identify whether there are any significant differences between time points. In the first paragraph of the Results, please clarify what is meant by “significant temporal changes”. Also, please either show VSMCs proliferate extensively or properly cite previous studies.
10. Extended Figures 3 and 4 do not add to the primary focus of the manuscript and could be deleted.
11. For Figure 5, additional data on the impact of loss of IL33 in PDGFRb+ cells on levels of cytokines in the vessel would provide insight into changes in the inflammatory environment. For Figure 5e, please present as bar graphs similar to Figure 5f, as it is currently difficult to assess differences between conditions. In Figure 5f, there is a trend towards higher neutrophil accumulation in response to loss of IL33 while macrophage numbers were downregulated. Please discuss potential impact on neointimal hyperplasia.
12. In Figure 7, additional flow cytometry data assessing OPN protein levels directly in macrophages and neutrophils isolated from arteries would strengthen the manuscript.

### Reviewer 2

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript the relationship between ST2 (IL1RL1)+ macrophages attracted by tissue resident stromal cells and vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC) in an endovascular injury model in male mice was demonstrated. The authors persuasively show that IL33 produced by the stromal cells induce a repair associated macrophage type that express Osteopontin that promotes VSMC proliferation and neointima formation. This manuscript shows convincing in vivo data with well executed transcriptomic and flow cytometry data.
The translational impact of these finding is a challenge since although the authors describe that these findings are relevant for coronary artery disease it is well known that cells in peripheral vascular tissues behave differently than in the heart. Furthermore, this model lacks any atherosclerotic background resulting in very suboptimal reflections. The presented research is thorough but for me unclear how relevant this is for human coronary PCA. Thorough additional research on the key factors in human disease samples is necessary to show the translational concept.
The concept of the ST2 macrophage/IL33 axes is well know and the link to osteopontin is described in other disease such as arthritis limiting the novelty of these findings.
A good explanation why only male mice are used should be clearly discussed.
Although the single cell sequencing data on these small samples is impressive I have some remarks; less than 10.000 cells for a heterogenous tissue such as the vessel wall (t0 timepoint) is affecting the reliability of these analysis. Interpretations of this datapoint should be very cautious. Why is only one gene (Ptprc) selected to represent the immune cells and why only use the Go pathway analysis and not other source such as KEGG or MSIG/DB?
Ly6c is a very general marker as the authors also describe, is this really the best marker for these inflammatory associated macrophages?
Figure 2P why is the vehicle completely occluded? This results in totally different processes than neointima formation and should be excluded from the analysis. How often is this observed in the experiments?
In some of the experiments it is not clearly described (for instance the histology in figure 1) which background and how many mice are used for the analysis.

### Reviewer 4

The study by Ping et al; investigates the of immunomodulatory mechanisms driving injury-responsive immune-stromal cell interactions in the realm of endovascular femoral artery injury. The study integrates time-resolved single cell RNA sequencing and multi-color flow cytometry to analyze the alterations in cellular components and cell-cell communication circuits within the injured femoral artery. The findings revealed a subset of ST2-expressing macrophages whose recruitment is fostered by injury-activated adventitial MSCs and plays a critical role in regulating VSMC proliferation. Also, MSC-derived IL-33 has been found to trigger the reparative phenotype of these ST2+ macrophages, that stimulate VSMC proliferation via OPN. Manipulating the IL33-ST2-OPN regulatory axis between MSCs and macrophages prevents NIH in the injured artery. Overall, the study is very interesting and is significantly supported by ample data and findings. However, several issues need to be addressed for considering for publication in Nat Comm. Nonetheless, the results reveal a novel mechanism addressing the wound healing process and post-injury neointima formation, targeting the MSC-macrophage interactions to prevent restenosis and other vascular diseases.
Comments
1. The introduction is very generic. A comprehensive survey of ST2-expressing macrophages and associated cells of interest emphasizing the immunomodulatory communications with resident MSCs along with underlying mechanisms are required to understand the rigor in this field. The introduction does not sufficiently highlight the study’s novelty or define the critical knowledge gap it intends to fill, limiting the reader’s understanding regarding the significance.
2. Density count of CD45 cells from multiple sections of each time frame would be appreciated for assessing the extend of WBC infiltration. Differential count and expression of WBC subsets are required to determine the nature/status of NIH. Also, measuring the difference in lumen diameter/aspect ratio will be helpful to quantify the extent of NIH.
3. In the results the authors mentioned that ‘Notably, a large number of vascular macrophages were detected at 7 days and 14 days post femoral artery injury……’. How are the vascular macrophages defined? What is their phenotypic signature? The tissue level characterization of these macrophages is crucial to understand their progression during the progression of pathology.
4. Similarly, ‘Their abundance eventually declined to baseline levels as vascular regeneration progressed by 28 days post-injury’. How was the vascular regeneration quantified? Tissue level data is required.
5. TREM2+ LLM are promising in RepMAC; however, the information regarding the pro-inflammatory counter part TREM1 would provide additional confirmation regarding the inflammatory/reparative status. TREM2-TREM1 ratio will be highly appreciated.
6. The figures and extended data are mixed up and not in the proper order which makes hard to follow the figures.
7. Upregulation of Il33 gene expression, rather than the changes in the abundance of Il33-expressing cells, appeared to contribute to the higher IL-33 levels observed in injured arteries. Explanation regarding the cell types and the underlying mechanisms for IL33 expression in the context of FAI.
8. Do inguinal adipose MSCs typically replicate the pathophysiology of MSCs from injured vascular tissue? Does the embryonic nature of HUVEC cells simulate the secretome content of injured ECs associated with mature blood vessels? How accurate and reproducible is the mechanical injury model? These models require further rationale and validations to correlate with the in vivo pathophysiology.
9. Screening data to quantify the content of CM is unavailable. The secretome analysis is required to provide mechanistic insights for CM-driven Il33 action.
10. Experimental details and data regarding the hydrogel composition and compatibility are missing.
11. The authors discussed the findings related to CAD; however, the model used was FA injury which would be a representation of PAD. Justification for the animal model is required. How the findings relate to clinical CVDs? What is the translational significance? What are the limitations of the study?
12. A section concluding the significance of key findings will be appreciated.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

POINT-BY-POINT RESPONSE TO REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, the authors report on the role of fibroblast-macrophage
interaction following femoral artery endovascular injury in mice. The authors
identify a pathway involving IL33-ST2-OPN in the regulation of macrophage
activity that promotes neointimal hyperplasia after injury. This study is data
intensive and experiments were generally well performed and well described.
However, the scRNAseq data are superficially analyzed/described, additional
data are needed to verify that perturbations have intended effects, gating
strategies for flow cytometry need to be reported and quantification strategies
justified, some data are overinterpreted and data presentation could be
improved.
Major comments
1. In the Introduction, authors claim that factors regulating macrophage
phenotype switching remain unclear. However, numerous studies implicate
many potential candidates including cytokines, signaling pathways, growth
factors. Please acknowledge this previous work and summarize current
understanding.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point and for
reminding us to reference the known roles of macrophages in this context. As
noted by the reviewer, previous studies have highlighted the functions of
cytokines and growth factors (e.g., IL-4, IL-13, IL-10, CSF-1, TGFβ, IGF-1) as
well as key downstream signaling mediators (e.g., STAT6, NFκB, PPARγ,
AMPK). We appreciate the comment that our initial description may have
oversimplified the current understanding of macrophage biology in this setting.
While these regulators and mechanisms have been implicated previously, the
detailed processes underlying macrophage “phenotypic switching” and its
regulatory control still remain poorly defined. In response, we have revised the
text to explicitly acknowledge prior work and clarify how our findings provide
new insights into how macrophages acquire a reparative phenotype in this
context. (Page 4, line 84-97)
2. Several datasets, including published scRNAseq data, were used in this
study. It is difficult to follow which dataset was used for analysis in several
figures. Please clarify the source of data used to generate each graph in each
Figure.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the careful reading of our manuscript and
for bringing this to our attention. We apologize for the omission of the relevant
scRNA-seq dataset information in the original version. We have now updated
the figures and the revised manuscript to include these details.
3. Flow cytometry data and presentation should be improved. First, enzymatic
tissue digestion causes significant cell death. Therefore, live/dead cell staining
should be used in all flow analysis to allow gating out of dead cells from analysis.
In addition, complete gating strategies for all flow cytometry analyses should be
provided either in main or supplementary Figures. When presenting flow data
as cell numbers, authors chose to normalize to per cm artery. Please justify this
choice, as the obvious change in artery thickness could be expected to
influence cell numbers. When presenting flow data as percentages, please
clarify the denominator cell population in the calculation (e.g. total cells or
immediate parent cell gate). Finally, please clarify which flow cytometry
antibodies were used to identify immune cell populations in Figure 1 and how
these correspond to the populations identified in the scRNAseq data.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestions regarding
methodologic information and data analysis, which provides an opportunity to
improve the clarity of our Methods section and to offer additional details.
In the flow assays in this work, we have gated out of dead cells based on
live/dead cell staining from analyses. With respect to methodological
information, the gating of live cells based on live/dead cell staining and
complete gating strategies for the flow cytometry experiments have been
included in the revised manuscript (see the Source Data Figure 1-3), as
suggested by the reviewer. We also have explicitly clarified the denominator
cell population used for each percentage calculation in the panels, figure
legends and the Methods section, thereby enhancing the clarity and
interpretability of our analyses. In addition, the complete information on flow
cytometry antibodies used for immune cell identification has been added to the
Methods section (Page 30, line 935-943, also see Table S6), and the cell type-
defining markers used in both flow cytometry and scRNA-seq analyses have
been specified in the revised manuscript (Table S6).
Regarding the reviewer’s comment on artery thickness and our choice to
normalize flow cytometry data per centimeter (cm) artery, our decision was
based on the unique characteristics of the mouse femoral artery and the
requirements of flow cytometry analysis, while also considering reported
approaches in the literature. Multiple normalization strategies have been
described, including normalization to artery number for analysis (PMID:
36899827), each with inherent limitations. Given the very small size of the
mouse femoral artery, normalization to tissue weight (per gram) is impractical
and introduces significant variability due to subtle differences in dissection or
surrounding adventitial fat. It is worthy to note that our samples were collected
at the early phase (D0, D2, and D7) post-injury when neointimal thickening is
not obvious, thereby minimizing the biological need to account for thickness as
a major factor for normalization. Moreover, enzymatic digestion of vascular
tissue into a single-cell suspension eliminates the tissue’s three-dimensional
structure, making post-digestion measurements of thickness or volume
unfeasible.
To address these challenges and ensure uniformity, we employed a
consistent sampling methodology. In the femoral artery wire-injury model, a
guide wire is inserted via the superficial femoral artery branch and advanced
distally to induce injury, after which the branch is ligated. For flow cytometry,
we consistently harvested a precisely defined 1 cm segment of the femoral
artery, measured proximally from the ligated branch junction. This approach
provided high reproducibility and ensured uniform sample collection across all
experiments.
4. scRNAseq analysis is overall superficial and/or incomplete. For data in
Figure 1 and Extended Figure 1, please provide a more complete list of marker
genes that differentiate both major cell clusters and immune cell subclusters for
all datasets analyzed. Along these lines, please discuss how CD72 and CD63
were chosen as markers to discriminate macrophage clusters; these markers
do not appear to be differentially expressed to a substantial level in the single
cell data. For all pathway analyses, please provide complete gene list as
supportive data for each pathway identified.
Response: We thank for the reviewer for these constructive comments and
suggestions. In response, we have now provided a complete list of marker
genes used to identify the major cell clusters and immune cell subclusters in
our scRNA-seq datasets (Table S6). For pathway analyses, the complete gene
lists for each pathway identified has been provided in Table S8.
Regarding our rationale for selecting CD63 and CD72 to differentiate
macrophage subclusters in this study, our selection was based on two major
considerations:
1) The primary reason was the need to identify robust cell surface markers that
could be used to establish a flow cytometry protocol for the analysis and
isolation of macrophage subclusters. Our scRNA-seq analysis revealed
CD63 and CD72 were among the top selectively expressed markers in the
injury-associated reparative macrophage subcluster. A full list of cell
membrane marker genes supporting the selection of CD63 and CD72 is
provided in Table S7. Leveraging their selective expression, we developed
a flow cytometry strategy using commercially available antibodies, enabling
both the analysis and isolation of these macrophage subclusters from
injured arteries. This approach was further validated by our observation that
the abundance of CD63⁺CD72⁺ macrophages significantly increased during
the repair stages post artery injury (Fig. 2h-j), coinciding with the time when
reparative macrophages are expected to predominate.
2) In addition to their suitability as cell surface markers, CD63 and CD72 are
functionally relevant to macrophage biology. CD63 is broadly involved in
extracellular vesicle formation and secretion, which are critical for tissue
repair and immune modulation (PMID: 40537510). Emerging evidence also
implicates CD72 in promoting macrophage polarization toward an anti-
inflammatory phenotype，which is one of the key features for reparative
macrophages (PMID: 34100920). Thus, CD63 and CD72 may serve as
“functional” markers of this newly identified injury-associated macrophage
subcluster, providing a promising direction for future mechanistic studies.
In summary, CD63 and CD72 rank among the top differentially expressed
cell surface makers between macrophage subclusters, and their selective and
consistent expression at both the mRNA level (scRNA-seq) and protein level
(flow cytometry) makes them highly useful markers across a broad range of
experiments conducted in this study.
For pseudotime analysis, cluster 1 macrophages are distributed across all
pseudotime branches. Please discuss the potential significance of the
presence of this apparently pro-inflammatory population over all pseudotime
states. Since cluster 2 macrophages tend to have higher pseudotimes, one
could infer that there may be a transition from cluster 1 to 2 macrophages.
Please discuss. For Monocle 3 analyses, please indicate which cluster was
selected as starting cluster. In addition to the pseudotime analysis, scRNA
velocity analysis would provide additional insight into potential cell state
transitions.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions regarding
our scRNA-seq analysis and data presentation. In response, we have revised
these sections as follows:
1) We agree that the observation of Cluster 1 macrophages persisting across
all pseudotime states is noteworthy, as it challenges a strictly linear
'inflammatory to reparative' transition model. This distribution likely reflects
a more dynamic and complex process. We hypothesize that Cluster 1
represent a continuously replenished population of pro-inflammatory
macrophages, either newly recruited to the injury site or maintained in a
low-level activated state. The coexistence of inflammatory and reparative
macrophage populations suggests that macrophage phenotypic transitions
during tissue repair do not occur as a simple binary switch but instead
reflect a dynamic equilibrium in which both macrophage subsets coexist
and remain functionally active. As suggested, we have expanded the
Discussion to include this interpretation (Page 17, line 503-505).
2) We agree with the reviewer that the higher pseudotimes of Cluster 2
macrophages strongly suggest a transition from Cluster 1 to Cluster 2.
Conceptually, pseudotime trajectory analysis is designed to model the
continuous progression of cells along a differentiation or activation pathway.
Accordingly, we have revised the Discussion to include this interpretation
(Page 17, line 503-505).
3) For the Monocle 3 analyses, Cluster 3 (monocytes) was selected as the
starting cluster, which is now indicated in the revised Extended Data Fig.
3c.
4) As suggested, scRNA velocity analysis has been performed to provide
additional insights into potential cell state transitions. Specifically, the
results support a directional flow from the pro-inflammatory cluster (Cluster
1) toward the reparative cluster (Cluster 2) (Revision Fig.1). Furthermore,
the velocity analysis revealed more complex dynamics: monocytes
primarily differentiate into the pro-inflammatory macrophage cluster
(Cluster 1); there is bidirectional interconversion between the pro-
inflammatory (Cluster 1) and reparative (Cluster 2) clusters, indicating that
these phenotypes are not fixed but rather represent reversible states
modulated by the tissue microenvironment; and the homeostatic
macrophage cluster primarily undergoes self-renewal, with a minor
potential contribution from the reparative cluster. These new findings have
been included in the revised Fig. 2e.

substantiate this claim.

and could be deleted.

Extended Data Figures 3 and 4, and streamlined the manuscript accordingly.

on levels of cytokines in the vessel would provide insight into changes in the

to Figure 5f, as it is currently difficult to assess differences between conditions.
In Figure 5f, there is a trend towards higher neutrophil accumulation in response
to loss of IL33 while macrophage numbers were downregulated. Please discuss

We thank the reviewer for this comment. We interpret the increase in
neutrophils observed following IL-33 deficiency as a potential compensatory
inflammatory response. Neutrophils, as key pro-inflammatory cells, are
predominantly involved in the early phase of vascular injury, when the
inflammatory response is at its peak (PMID: 11864917, 40492585, 10669628).
Together with the data regarding the compassion of macrophages and
neutrophils, we think that the contribution of neutrophils to late-stage neointimal
hyperplasia is likely less significant than that of macrophages, which at this
stage have largely acquired a reparative phenotype. As suggested, we have
expanded the Discussion to address this point (Page 12, line 350-353).

directly in macrophages and neutrophils isolated from arteries would strengthen

(Revision Fig. 7b). These data are consistent with scRNA-seq analysis in Fig.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed
reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training
in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career
Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript the relationship between ST2 (IL1RL1)+ macrophages
attracted by tissue resident stromal cells and vascular smooth muscle cells
(VSMC) in an endovascular injury model in male mice was demonstrated. The
authors persuasively show that IL33 produced by the stromal cells induce a
repair associated macrophage type that express Osteopontin that promotes
VSMC proliferation and neointima formation. This manuscript shows convincing
in vivo data with well executed transcriptomic and flow cytometry data.
1. The translational impact of these finding is a challenge since although the
authors describe that these findings are relevant for coronary artery disease it
is well known that cells in peripheral vascular tissues behave differently than
in the heart. Furthermore, this model lacks any atherosclerotic background
resulting in very suboptimal reflections. The presented research is thorough
but for me unclear how relevant this is for human coronary PCA. Thorough
additional research on the key factors in human disease samples is necessary
to show the translational concept.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments regarding the
translational impact of our study. We fully agree that biological differences exist
between peripheral and coronary arteries, and acknowledge that our model
lacks an atherosclerotic background.
However, we would like to clarify the primary objective of this study and the
relevance of our model. The focus of this work is to investigate the specific
pathological process of neointimal hyperplasia-related restenosis, which is a
major long-term complication following PCI, rather than to model the entire
course of coronary artery disease. PCI procedures, including balloon
angioplasty and stent implantation widely adopted clinical treatments of
coronary atherosclerosis, inevitably cause mechanical injury to the vessel wall,
leading to endothelial denudation and the aberrant proliferation and migration
of vascular smooth muscle cells, the key pathological events underlying
restenosis. Mouse arteries, however, unlike those of larger animals such as
pigs, rabbits and rats, are too small for transluminal injury with a balloon. The
femoral artery wire-injury model faithfully recapitulates this mechanical injury
process. Although femoral arteries differ from coronary arteries, femoral artery
injury model which is conducted by dilation of the mouse femoral artery by
intraluminal insertion of a larger wire, is widely accepted and reliable for
studying critical aspects of restenosis, including endothelial repair, VSMC
proliferation, and neointimal formation. Its major advantage lies in its ability to
isolate the mechanical injury-induced restenosis process from confounding
factors like an atherosclerotic background, thereby enabling precise
investigation of the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms. This model
is widely used to analyze genetically modified mice in studies on the
pathophysiology of post-angioplasty restenosis since it was established at 2000
(PMID: 11040113). We have also added supporting literature to further
substantiate the validity of this model for restenosis research (PMID: 39873228).
Nevertheless, we recognize the biological differences between peripheral and
coronary arteries and have now added a discussion of these limitations in the
revised manuscript.
Due to the limitation in accessing human artery samples post PCI
treatments, we alternatively collected plasma samples from patients with or
without in-stent restenosis (ISR) after coronary stent implantation to validate
the clinical relevance of our findings. Plasma protein levels of IL-33 and
osteopontin (OPN) were then correlated with the patients’ angiographic
outcomes. ELISA results revealed that both IL-33 and OPN levels were
significantly higher in patients who developed restenosis (ISR) compared to
those without restenosis (Non-ISR, Revision Figure 11). These new human
data provide important clinical evidence, suggesting that the IL-33–ST2–OPN
axis is not only important in our mouse model but also relevant in the
complication following PCI in patients.

or without in-stent restenosis (ISR). (also see the Fig. 4g and Fig. 7i in the
revised manuscript)

2.The concept of the ST2 macrophage/IL33 axes is well know and the link to
osteopontin is described in other disease such as arthritis limiting the novelty
of these findings.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this question and for providing the
opportunity to highlight the novelty of our findings. We agree that IL-33 signaling
has been reported to regulate macrophage functions (PMID: 32644975,
32272082, 29420261). Likewise, OPN has been implicated in various
pathological conditions, including neointimal hyperplasia of arteriovenous
fistulae (PMID: 36646166). Previous studies have also described an IL-33–
ST2–Amphiregulin axis in Th2 cells, which then promotes the OPN production
of eosinophils in the context of allergic airway inflammation and fibrosis (PMID:
29958800). However, to our knowledge, no prior work has demonstrated a
direct relationship between the IL-33–ST2 axis and OPN expression in
macrophages. In this study, we show that IL-33/ST2 signaling are crucial in the
recruitment of reparative macrophages and directly regulates OPN expression
in this macrophage subset, a key cell type driving vascular repair and
remodeling. This direct cellular and molecular connection defines a previously
unrecognized mechanism underlying neointimal hyperplasia, thereby
distinguishing our work from earlier studies.
3.A good explanation why only male mice are used should be clearly discussed.
Response：We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the use of only
male mice in this study. This decision was based on the well-documented
influence of sex hormones, particularly estrogen, on vascular physiology and
pathology. Estrogen exerts protective effects on the vasculature, including
modulation of vascular injury responses and inhibition of vascular smooth
muscle cell proliferation. Including female mice, with their fluctuating estrogen
levels, would introduce additional biological variability and potentially confound
the interpretation of our mechanistic findings, particularly with respect to the
specific molecular pathways under investigation.
4.Although the single cell sequencing data on these small samples is
impressive I have some remarks; less than 10.000 cells for a heterogenous
tissue such as the vessel wall (t0 timepoint) is affecting the reliability of these
analysis. Interpretations of this datapoint should be very cautious. Why is only
one gene (Ptprc) selected to represent the immune cells. why only use the Go
pathway analysis and not other source such as KEGG or MSIG/DB?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive comments on our
scRNA-seq analysis and data presentation. In response to the most important
point raised, although the Sham group (D0) contained fewer cells (5,960)
compared to D2 (11,016) and D7 (10,539), all quality control metrics confirm
excellent data quality, and the biological conclusions remain robust. Our
detailed responses to this point are as follows:
1. Regarding cell number and sample derivation, each sample was derived
from a pool of multiple mice (D0, 12 mice; D2 and D7, 6 mice each group).
The lower cell number in the Sham group reflects the biological context:
blood vessels in the normal condition remain intact with minimal immune
cell infiltration, naturally yielding fewer isolated cells compared with injured
states, which show strong immune responses.
2. With respect to quality control metrics, the Sham group showed
comparable genome alignment rate (91.3%) and transcriptome alignment
rate (77.7%) to the other two groups (92.9%/79.2% and 92.7%/79.5%),
indicating no significant difference in data validity. Q30 base quality
(UMI >97.5%, RNA reads >94.6%) and valid barcode ratio (95.4%) meet
the widely-accepted standards for single-cell sequencing and alignment.
For cell data integrity, the higher sequencing saturation (82.4%) in Sham
group demonstrates sufficient transcriptome coverage, with minimal benefit
from additional sequencing depth, and the significantly higher mean reads
per cell (45,728 vs ~28,000 in the other two groups) ensures robust
transcript abundance per cell. The slightly lower median genes per cell
(1,660 vs ~2,300 in the other two groups) likely reflects the quiescent
transcriptional state of control cells rather than technical artifacts.
Importantly, the total genes detected (22,850) were comparable to FAI
groups (23,000–24,000), confirming comprehensive capture of the gene
repertoire.
In conclusion, the Sham group data fully meet single-cell research
standards, and the difference in cell numbers does not compromise our core
findings. Full QC details (UMI counts, alignment rates, and other metrics) are
provided in the Table S10 of the revised manuscript for verification.
To clarify our use of Ptprc gene for immune cell identification, Ptprc gene
encodes CD45 protein, a classical and one of the most widely used marker for
hematopoietic immune cells. In addition, we employed multiple lineage-specific
markers to define distinct immune cell types, as detailed in the Table S6.
We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestion regarding pathway
enrichment. In response, we have updated our pathway analysis to include
KEGG and MSIG/DB pathway analyses. The results are consistent with our
original GO pathway analysis, again highlighting the relative enrichment of
genes involved in collagen degradation, extracellular matrix organization
pathways in Cluster 2 macrophages. These new results have been organized
and incorporated into the Table S11.
5.Ly6c is a very general marker as the authors also describe, is this really the
best marker for these inflammatory associated macrophages?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment, which provided an
opportunity to clarify our rationale for selecting LY6C to distinguish pro-
inflammatory macrophage subcluster in this study. Our selection was guided by
two main considerations. First, LY6C is a widely-used surface marker that
enables the development of a flow cytometry protocol for both the analysis and
isolation of macrophage subclusters. Second, LY6C is reported as a marker for
pro-inflammatory macrophages (PMID: 38698086), aligning with the molecular
and cellular characteristics of LY6C+ macrophage subcluster identified in our
data. Taken together, these features make LY6C a highly practical and
functionally relevant marker for a broad range of analyses in this study.
6.Figure 2P why is the vehicle completely occluded? This results in totally
different processes than neointima formation and should be excluded from the
analysis. How often is this observed in the experiments?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the careful evaluation of the histological
results presented in original Figure 2P. We agree that the image originally
shown for the Vehicle control displays near-complete, though not total (the
remaining lumen area is now indicated in Revision Fig. 12a) vascular occlusion.
This represents an extreme pathological manifestation and deviates from the
typical neointimal hyperplasia process that is the focus of our study.
We initially selected this image for its visual clarity in illustrating severe
vascular pathology; however, we acknowledge that it may be misleading. To
enhance data transparency, we now provide all six images corresponding to
the Vehicle samples from six mice used for the statistical analysis, thereby
illustrating the average pathological status across all examined animals.
(Revision Fig. 12b). In addition, to more accurately represent the average
pathological state of the Vehicle control group, we have replaced the image in
Figure 2P with one that is representative of neointimal hyperplasia observed in
this group.

b, Additional H&E staining of the other 5 vehicle-treated samples used for

7.In some of the experiments it is not clearly described (for instance the
histology in figure 1) which background and how many mice are used for the
analysis.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out and apologize for the
omission of this information in the original manuscript. Details regarding the
background and number of mice used in this study have now been included in
the figure legends of the revised figures throughout the manuscript.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
The study by Ping et al; investigates the of immunomodulatory mechanisms
driving injury-responsive immune-stromal cell interactions in the realm of
endovascular femoral artery injury. The study integrates time-resolved single
cell RNA sequencing and multi-color flow cytometry to analyze the alterations
in cellular components and cell-cell communication circuits within the injured
femoral artery. The findings revealed a subset of ST2-expressing macrophages
whose recruitment is fostered by injury-activated adventitial MSCs and plays a
critical role in regulating VSMC proliferation. Also, MSC-derived IL-33 has been
found to trigger the reparative phenotype of these ST2+ macrophages, that
stimulate VSMC proliferation via OPN. Manipulating the IL33-ST2-OPN
regulatory axis between MSCs and macrophages prevents NIH in the injured
artery. Overall, the study is very interesting and is significantly supported by
ample data and findings. However, several issues need to be addressed for
considering for publication in Nat Comm. Nonetheless, the results reveal a
novel mechanism addressing the wound healing process and post-injury
neointima formation, targeting the MSC-macrophage interactions to prevent
restenosis and other vascular diseases.
Comments
1. The introduction is very generic. A comprehensive survey of ST2-expressing
macrophages and associated cells of interest emphasizing the
immunomodulatory communications with resident MSCs along with underlying
mechanisms are required to understand the rigor in this field. The introduction
does not sufficiently highlight the study’s novelty or define the critical knowledge
gap it intends to fill, limiting the reader’s understanding regarding the
significance.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive comments on the
Introduction. To better highlight the contribution of our findings to the current
understanding of MSC-Immune cell immunomodulatory interactions, we have
added a few lines summarizing reported studies on ST2-expressing
macrophages and other immune cells in their communication with resident
MSCs. These additions, included in the revised manuscript (Page 4, line 93-
97), further emphasize the involvement of AKT (PMID: 34982959), ERK1/2
(PMID: 32272082), and GATA3 (PMID: 34644537) signaling pathways. Our
findings highlight a newly identified IL-33–ST2–OPN regulatory axis, revealing
a key communication mechanism by which MSCs modulate pro-repair immune
responses in macrophages.
2. Density count of CD45 cells from multiple sections of each time frame would
be appreciated for assessing the extend of WBC infiltration. Differential count
and expression of WBC subsets are required to determine the nature/status of
NIH. Also, measuring the difference in lumen diameter/aspect ratio will be
helpful to quantify the extent of NIH.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestions. To better
characterize neointimal hyperplasia (NIH), we quantified CD45+ cells and
lumen diameter/aspect ratio across the time course. Our results showed that
day 2 post-FAI (D2) had the most abundant infiltrated immune cells and largest
lumen diameter/aspect ratio, identifying it as the most active inflammatory stage,
while both parameters gradually returned to baseline by day 28 post-FAI (D28),
indicating completion of repair (Revision Fig. 13a-b). Using scRNA-seq data,
we further evaluated functional activity scores of eight main leukocyte subsets,
which revealed dynamic changes in specific immune cell populations during the
process of neointimal hyperplasia (Revision Fig. 13c). In addition, we provided
lumen diameter/aspect ratio data for each animal assays as suggested
(Revision Fig. 13d-i).

3. In the results the authors mentioned that ‘Notably, a large number of vascular
macrophages were detected at 7 days and 14 days post femoral artery
injury……’. How are the vascular macrophages defined? What is their
phenotypic signature? The tissue level characterization of these macrophages
is crucial to understand their progression during the progression of pathology.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to the definition of vascular
macrophages. In this study, the term “vascular macrophages” referred to
macrophages residing within the vasculature, which were the primary target cell
population examined. Consistent with conventional definitions, these cells were
identified as CD45+CD11b+F4/80+ using flow cytometry. To prevent potential
misunderstanding, we have revised the manuscript by replacing “vascular
macrophages” with a more precise description throughout the text.
4. Similarly, ‘Their abundance eventually declined to baseline levels as vascular
regeneration progressed by 28 days post-injury’. How was the vascular
regeneration quantified? Tissue level data is required.
Response: We thank for the reviewer for bringing this to our attention. To
quantify vascular regeneration, we utilized established histological metrics of
neointimal hyperplasia (NIH) and including vessel lumen diameter-to-aspect
ratio, and immune cell infiltration (Revision Fig. 13a,b), thereby addressing the
reviewer’s request for tissue-level data.
Consistent with prior studies (PMID: 25867187), our data showed that
immune cell infiltration peaks by 2 days post-injury then declines to basal levels
at 28 days post-injury (Revision Fig. 13b), with proliferation of resident cells
such as smooth muscle cells and endothelial cells, following a similar timeline
(PMID: 34474592). These results have been included in the revised manuscript
(Extended Data Fig. 1a-c in the revised manuscript).
5.TREM2+ LLM are promising in RepMAC; however, the information regarding
the pro-inflammatory counter part TREM1 would provide additional
confirmation regarding the inflammatory/reparative status. TREM2-TREM1
ratio will be highly appreciated.
Response: We thank the reviewer for bringing this to our attention. As
suggested, we performed an analysis of Trem1 and Trem2 expression in
macrophages at different time points based on our scRNA-seq datasets, and
the results showed that Trem1-expressing macrophages continuously
increased post-injury, rising from 8.3% to 27% at 2 days post-injury (D2), and
reaching 29.7% at 7 days post-injury (D7). This suggests that a pro-
inflammatory macrophage population persists in the early phase of the vascular
repair process. While Trem2-expressing macrophages increased sharply post-
injury, rising from 17.7% to a peak of 66.4% at D2, before decreasing to 47%
at D7 (Revision Figure 14). These results described the distinct dynamic
changes of these two macrophage populations during vascular injury and repair,
suggesting potential different functional roles of these Trem1+ and Trem2+
macrophages in this setting.

macrophages following FAI. (also see the Extended Data Fig. 3j in the
revised manuscript)

6. The figures and extended data are mixed up and not in the proper order
which makes hard to follow the figures.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the confusion regarding the
figure and extended data order. We have carefully reorganized all main figures
and extended data figures in the revised manuscript.
7. Upregulation of Il33 gene expression, rather than the changes in the
abundance of Il33-expressing cells, appeared to contribute to the higher IL-33
levels observed in injured arteries. Explanation regarding the cell types and the
underlying mechanisms for IL33 expression in the context of FAI.
Response: In response, we performed scRNA-seq analysis,
immunofluorescence staining with anti-IL-33 antibodies and flow cytometry
using the Il33GFP reporter mouse model to examine Il33 expression pattern in
injured arteries (Fig. 4b-d and Extended Data Fig. 6a in the revised manuscript).
These analyses showed that Il33 expression was predominantly detected in
PDGFR+ MSC subsets located in the adventitial layer.
To investigate the regulatory mechanisms of Il33 expression upon FAI, we
co-cultured Il33-expressing PDGFR+ MSCs isolated from inguinal adipose
tissue with conditioned media (CM) derived from mechanically injured cultured
endothelial cells (HUVECs). CM from injured HUVECs (CM_Inj) induced a 2-3-
fold increase in Il33 expression compared with CM from uninjured HUVECs
(CM_Nor) (Fig. 4i). Bulk RNA-seq analysis of MSCs after FAI using Gene Set
Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) revealed enrichment of the “NFB signaling
pathway” and related pathways, including “TNF signaling pathway” and “IL-17
signaling pathway”. Consistently, CM_Inj activated IKK-NFB signaling
pathway in MSCs, as evidenced by the elevated levels of phosphorylated
IKK/ and p65, while Il33 induction was blocked by the p65 inhibitor JSH23 or
Rela knockdown (Fig. 4o,q). Sequence analysis of murine Il33 promoter
identified 3 putative p65 binding sites (B.S.-1~3). Chromatin
Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays confirmed that CM_Inj enhanced p65
binding at B.S-2 and -3, suggesting that NFB signaling directly regulates Il33
transcription in MSCs (Fig. 4r). Together, we found that MSCs serve as the
main source of IL-33 in arteries and injury-upregulated Il33 transcription in
MSCs are driven by the activated NFB signaling pathway during FAI.
8. Do inguinal adipose MSCs typically replicate the pathophysiology of MSCs
from injured vascular tissue? Does the embryonic nature of HUVEC cells
simulate the secretome content of injured ECs associated with mature blood
vessels? How accurate and reproducible is the mechanical injury model? These
models require further rationale and validations to correlate with the in vivo
pathophysiology.
Response: We thank for the reviewer’s comment regarding the relevance of our
in vitro models to in vivo pathophysiology, particularly their use in uncovering
the underlying mechanisms. To address this, we compared the top 10
upregulated genes identified in vivo from scRNA-seq of endothelial cells and
bulk RNA-seq of MSCs with gene expression in the cells using in our in vitro
models. We found that these genes were also significantly upregulated in
injured HUVECs and MSCs treated by CM_injured (Revision Fig. 15a,b).
These results indicate that our in vitro models faithfully recapitulate key transcriptional
responses observed in vivo, thereby validating their use for dissecting the
cellular and molecular mechanisms of vascular repair.

9. Screening data to quantify the content of CM is unavailable. The secretome

Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. To
investigate the mechanisms underlying the transcriptional activation of Il33, we
performed a comprehensive secretome analysis of CM derived from endothelial
cell lines using mass spectrum. The full list of identified proteins is provided in

cells actives Il33 expression in MSCs through the NFκB pathway. Consistent
with this hypothesis, our analysis revealed increased levels of four secreted
proteins known to activate NFκB signaling, including the immunoregulator β2-
microglobulin (B2M), macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), the
chemokine CXCL5, and integrin β1 (ITGB1) (Revision Fig.16a-c) (PMID:
32059688, 34758833, 34242901, 30792394). These results suggest that these
factors may mediate the activation of NFκB-IL-33 axis in MSCs in response to
endothelial injury.

10. Experimental details and data regarding the hydrogel composition and
compatibility are missing.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of hydrogel
composition and compatibility details. In this study, we used a 20% (w/v)
Pluronic F127 hydrogel, a well-established thermosensitive triblock copolymer
that remains liquid at 4 °C and rapidly gels at 37 °C, enabling precise local
delivery after surgery. The solution was prepared in sterile PBS, stirred
overnight at 4 °C, and mixed with siRNA (30 μg) on ice to maintain its liquid
state until application. Macroscopic and histological analyses confirmed
effective gel formation and local retention at the injured artery, with no apparent
diffusion. Pluronic F127 is widely validated as a biocompatible, low-toxicity
polymer, supporting the safety of our delivery approach. These methodological
details have been added to the Methods section in the revised manuscript.
11. The authors discussed the findings related to CAD; however, the model
used was FA injury which would be a representation of PAD. Justification for
the animal model is required. How the findings relate to clinical CVDs? What is
the translational significance? What are the limitations of the study?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comments regarding the translational
impact of our study, which were also raised by Reviewer 3. We would like to
clarify that the primary objective of this work was to investigate the pathological
process of neointimal hyperplasia-related restenosis, a major complication
following PAD, rather than to model the entire course of CAD. The femoral
artery wire-injury model is widely accepted for this purpose, as it faithfully
recapitulates the mechanical injury process and allows focused investigation of
key events such as SMC proliferation, endothelial repair, and neointimal
formation. Mouse arteries, however, unlike those of larger animals such as pigs,
rabbits and rats, are too small for transluminal injury with a balloon. Although
femoral arteries differ from coronary arteries, femoral artery injury model which
is conducted by dilation of the mouse femoral artery by intraluminal insertion of
a larger wire, is widely accepted and reliable for studying critical aspects of
restenosis, including endothelial repair, VSMC proliferation, and neointimal
formation. This model is widely used to analyze genetically modified mice in
studies on the pathophysiology of post-angioplasty restenosis since it was
created at 2000 (PMID: 11040113). Its strength lies in isolating mechanical
injury–induced restenosis from confounding factors such as atherosclerosis,
thereby enabling precise dissection of the underlying cellular and molecular
mechanisms with translational implications. Moreover, our findings on the IL-
33–ST2–OPN axis, together with the demonstrated efficacy of hydrogel-
mediated siRNA silencing of Il33 or Spp1 in preventing restenosis, conceptually
suggest the potential of this approach for clinical translation.
In addition, a paragraph outlining the limitations of the study has been added
to the revised manuscript (Page 19, line 545-549).
12. A section concluding the significance of key findings will be appreciated.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We have added
a section in the revised manuscript highlighting the significance of our findings
(Page 19, Line 550-557).
“We reveal a previously unrecognized MSC–macrophage signaling axis that
shapes vascular repair after injury. Injury-activated adventitial MSCs release IL-
33 to recruit and activate reparative ST2+ macrophages, which drive VSMC
proliferation via OPN secretion. Targeting this IL-33–ST2–OPN pathway offers
a promising strategy to limit neointimal hyperplasia and prevent restenosis.
These findings significantly advance our understanding of how immune–
stromal interactions regulate tissue repair, particularly in the vascular context,
and uncover MSC–macrophage crosstalk as a potential therapeutic target for
preventing restenosis and related vascular diseases.”
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have satisfactorily addressed most of my concerns and the paper is
improved. I have a few remaining minor concerns:
1. I may be missing them, but I am not able to find complete gating strategies for each
flow cytometry assay in either the main or supplementary figures. These must be
included to allow readers to judge the quality of the data.
Response: We thank the reviewer for brining this to our attention. The gating strategies
were presented in the Source data file in last revision. To make it more convient for
accessible, we have added the gating strategies into Supplemental Figure 9 for the
reviewer’s reference.
2. In response to my comments on the pseudotime analysis, the authors state “The
coexistence of inflammatory and reparative macrophage populations suggests that
macrophage phenotypic transitions during tissue repair do not occur as a simple binary
switch but instead reflect a dynamic equilibrium in which both macrophage subsets
coexist and remain functionally active. As suggested, we have expanded the Discussion
to include this interpretation (Page 17, line 503-505)”, on page 6 of their rebuttal letter.
The discussion added does adequately address this issue. Please add verbiage similar
to what was provided in the rebuttal letter.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. In response, we have
revised the text to include this discussion as suggested (Page 17, line 484-491).
3. Although the authors have added a limitations paragraph, potential differences in
phenotypes of cells used for in vitro experiments compared to arterial cells and
incomplete understanding of the regulation of macrophage phenotype shifts observed
should be added to this paragraph.
Response: In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have expanded the limitations
paragraph to include the highlighted points (Page 18, line 533-536).
“In addition, the endothelial cell lines used in our in vitro experiments may not fully
recapitulate the phenotypic features of arterial endothelial cells. Finally, the mechanisms
governing macrophage phenotypic transtition in this context remain incompletey defined
and warrant future investigation.”
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports.
This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review
and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review
manuscripts.
Response: Many thanks.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have clearly performed a comprehensive and thoughtful revision that has
considerably strengthened the manuscript. Most reviewer concerns have been
addressed in a satisfactory and convincing manner. I therefore support publication of this
revised version.
Response: Many thanks.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
The revised manuscript has successfully addressed the comments, recommendations
and suggestions provided during initial review. The revised manuscript has been included
with conceptual clarity, additional data, methodological details and interpretations. The
revised manuscript can be accepted for publication in Nature Communications.
Response: Many thanks.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.
